reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children, and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: Dextrocardia denotes a heart whose apex points to the right hemithorax and must be distinguished from dextroposition, where an extracardiac process merely displaces a normally formed heart rightward.

The clinical significance depends entirely on the accompanying visceral situs: dextrocardia with situs inversus usually accompanies a structurally normal heart, whereas dextrocardia with situs solitus carries a high burden of complex congenital heart disease.
Dextrocardia with situs solitus (isolated dextrocardia) is frequently associated with congenitally corrected transposition, ventricular septal defect and pulmonary stenosis.
A segmental sequential analysis of atrial situs, ventricular loop and great-artery connection is essential to characterise the malformation before any intervention.
On examination the apex beat and heart sounds are maximal on the right, and the ECG shows reversed praecordial R-wave progression with abnormal frontal axis unless leads are repositioned.
Right-sided praecordial leads or mirror-image electrode placement are required to obtain an interpretable ECG.
Dextroposition from right pulmonary hypoplasia, diaphragmatic hernia or large left effusion should be excluded before labelling true dextrocardia.
Association with primary ciliary dyskinesia should be considered when dextrocardia accompanies situs inversus and chronic respiratory disease.
reference.pathophysiology: Dextrocardia arises from abnormal direction of embryonic cardiac looping and its interaction with overall body situs. In normal development the straight heart tube undergoes rightward (D-loop) looping so the morphological right ventricle lies rightward and the apex swings left. When looping and situs are coordinately reversed, as in situs inversus totalis, the apex points right but atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial concordance is preserved in mirror image, usually yielding a normal heart. When cardiac position is reversed independently of visceral situs (dextrocardia with situs solitus), there is a mismatch between the direction of looping and atrial arrangement, which strongly predisposes to segmental discordances such as congenitally corrected transposition and to septal and outflow malformations. True dextrocardia is thus an intrinsic developmental malposition, in contrast to dextroposition, where a normally formed and normally looped heart is secondarily shifted rightward by loss of lung volume or a space-occupying process in the left hemithorax.
additionalDifferentials: dextroposition from pulmonary hypoplasia or agenesis
mediastinal shift from large left pleural effusion or pneumothorax
situs inversus totalis with mirror-image heart
isolated levocardia with abdominal situs anomaly
congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries
additionalInvestigations: transthoracic echocardiography with full segmental analysis
chest radiograph localising apex, gastric bubble and aortic arch
ECG with right-sided or mirror-image lead placement
abdominal ultrasound to define visceral situs and spleen number
cross-sectional cardiac imaging (CT or MRI) for complex anatomy
assessment for primary ciliary dyskinesia when situs inversus coexists with respiratory disease
genetic and laterality evaluation in selected cases
redFlags: neonatal cyanosis or heart failure indicating complex associated congenital heart disease
rapid respiratory distress suggesting dextroposition from an acute intrathoracic process
murmur, abnormal pulses or failure to thrive in an infant with rightward apex
chronic sinopulmonary disease pointing to primary ciliary dyskinesia
planned surgery or line placement where malposition risks a wrong-side procedure
reference.prognosis: Dextrocardia associated with situs inversus and an otherwise normal heart has an excellent outlook, whereas dextrocardia with situs solitus often accompanies complex congenital heart disease and carries a prognosis governed by those lesions and their reparability. Outcome therefore ranges from normal life expectancy to that of severe cyanotic congenital heart disease.
pitfalls: Confusing true dextrocardia with dextroposition and missing the underlying pulmonary or diaphragmatic cause.
Interpreting the standard-placement ECG as ischaemic or lead-reversed artefact.
Assuming a normal heart without performing full segmental echocardiography, especially in situs solitus.
Overlooking congenitally corrected transposition and its late complications.
Failing to alert procedural teams to the reversed cardiac position.
